San Pedro Creek · Linda Mar · Pacifica

What's polluting Pacifica State Beach?

San Pedro Creek test results, day by day

Pacifica State Beach at Linda Mar consistently ranks among the least healthy beaches on the California coast, and the contamination comes from San Pedro Creek. This page shows every water test since 2000 — San Mateo County Environmental Health's weekly monitoring and the Linda Mar Water Quality Coalition's four creek sites — alongside the conditions that shape how bad the pollution gets: rainfall, estimated creek flow, ground wetness, and temperature. The pollution has a source. These conditions raise and lower its levels. This page is updated as new results come in. The county's beach record here reaches back to 2000; its creek testing begins in September 2015; the coalition's four-site program begins in July 2024. The goal of this work is to find the source of the pollution, eliminate it, and make the beach safe to use. Use the filters to choose what is displayed. The views below the graph show the patterns in the data and explain them.

How to use the graph below
  • The graph opens with every raw sample: the coalition’s four creek sites (weekly since July 2024 — the density jump that summer is the coalition’s program beginning), the county’s creek station (weekly since 2015), and the county’s beach record (weekly since 2000). The sites average and Surfrider’s creek-mouth series are in the Samples row.
  • Red dots are samples over the health standard (dashed line); orange dots passed. With Color by source on, dots keep their source’s color instead — judge by the dashed lines. Each gridline on the bacteria scale is ten times the one below it.
  • Estimated flow, ground wetness, and water temperature are calculated from rainfall and air temperature records, not measured — no instruments in the valley measure them directly. Methods describes how each estimate was checked.
  • Zoom with a two-finger pinch or Ctrl/⌘ + scroll. Turn layers on and off in the filters.

Patterns that may explain what happens in the creek. Selecting a view sets the graph above, explains what to look for, and offers a short tour of real examples from the record.

Views

Ask the data a question

Years of testing point to a handful of things that actually move the creek — warmth, rain and its aftermath, the winter’s stored water, when and where the sample was taken, and, at the beach, the tide. Each question below puts one of them to the record: days are split into three groups, from low to high, and the typical result of each group is compared. Bars that climb mean the factor matters; bars that look alike mean it doesn’t — and the questions that show nothing are reported just as plainly. Each card names the data it uses and explains what the pattern suggests.

Where this data comes from

Bacteria — County
San Mateo County Environmental Health weekly sampling, published through CEDEN: data.ca.gov — fecal indicator bacteria results (downloadable, API-accessible).
Bacteria — Coalition
The Coalition's four creek sites, weekly: lindamarwaterquality.org/test-results (Excel downloads).
Rainfall & air temperature
ERA5 weather-model records via Open-Meteo (free API; watershed point 37.585, −122.47).
Tides
NOAA CO-OPS harmonic predictions, Princeton/Half Moon Bay station 9414131 — the open-coast station nearest Linda Mar. (The SF Golden Gate gauge runs 30–65 minutes behind the coast; earlier versions of this page used it.)
Sewer spill reports
State Water Board CIWQS: sanitary sewer spill data files (City of Pacifica system, WDID 2SSO10100).
Gauged creeks used to check estimates
USGS water data — San Gregorio 11162500, Pescadero 11162570, Soquel 11160000, San Lorenzo 11160500, Pilarcitos 11162630.
Analysis code & assumptions
Every calculation, inference, and its validation: github.com/augers-co/pacifica-beach-water (see docs/inferences.md for the assumptions register).

Methods & definitions

Bacteria results
County weekly grab samples via CEDEN — creek: E. coli 2015→, enterococcus on some dates from spring 2026; beach: enterococcus 2000→ and E. coli 2001→. Coalition weekly samples at four creek sites (both organisms, 2024→), plus county LM5 taken the same mornings, from lindamarwaterquality.org. Replicates collapsed to the maximum. Values per 100 mL. The sites average shown is a calculated value: the geometric mean of whichever of the four sites were sampled that week (at least two required).
Standards
Freshwater E. coli 320; freshwater enterococcus 110; ocean enterococcus 104; ocean E. coli 320 (single-sample values). The map applies the standard matching each site and organism. These are health-based state standards, not choices made for this page: the freshwater values are California’s statewide Bacteria Provisions (State Water Board, 2018), adopted from EPA’s 2012 Recreational Water Quality Criteria, which swimmer-illness studies calibrated to a ceiling of about 32 gastrointestinal illnesses per 1,000 swimmers. The ocean enterococcus 104 is California’s beach standard (AB 411, 1997), the same line the county posts advisories on. Each single-sample value is the companion to a stricter primary test — a rolling geometric mean (freshwater E. coli 100, drawn with the Trend lines; ocean enterococcus 35).
Measurement noise
Two labs sampling the same reach the same morning agree on pass/fail 80% of the time (74 paired days; log–log r = 0.56). Single grabs carry ~±half-log noise; read patterns, not points.
Rain
ERA5 reanalysis daily precipitation at the watershed. No gauge exists in the valley.
Estimated flow (inferred from rain)
Ft = 0.90·Ft−1 + ½Pt + ½Pt−1. Checked against five comparable gauged coastal creeks: r = 0.69–0.73 (log–log daily). Like ground wetness, the scale is a unitless index — relative shape, not gauged flow; compare levels, not absolute numbers. The rain shadow (in the filters and the Rainstorms view) fades at the empirically fitted risk rate — excess exceedance halves every ~2.2 days — while flow halves every ~6.6 days. The gap is a finding: risk clears ~3× faster than the water recedes (first flush carries the load).
Ground wetness (inferred from rain)
An index of how much past storm water the ground is still holding, built with a standard hydrology technique — an antecedent wetness index. Each day it keeps 97% of the previous day’s value and adds a share of the previous day’s estimated flow, so storms fill it and it drains about 3% a day, taking months to empty. The scale has no units, because nothing in the valley measures groundwater (no wells, no gauge): 0 means fully drained, and the wettest winters on record reach about 300. Only comparisons carry meaning — twice the number means twice the stored water. Its rises and falls were checked against dry-season baseflow (= groundwater discharge) at the five analog creeks: r = 0.65–0.74. Formula: Gt = 0.97·Gt−1 + 0.10·Ft−1.
Water temperature (inferred from air)
No creek in the region has measured water temperature since 1979 — but San Gregorio Creek did, daily, 1965–1979. Fitting that record against the same weather-model air temperatures used here: water ≈ −1.6 + 1.05 × (7-day mean air), r = 0.85, typical error ±2°C over 3,932 paired days. That transfer, applied to Pacifica's air record, is the water-temperature presumption shown — labeled inferred, like every estimate on this page.
Rain vs normal (season running total)
Water-year cumulative rain vs the 1998–2026 day-of-season average. Summers after wet winters run ~3× summers after dry ones in rain-free weeks.
Sewer spills
State CIWQS reports, City of Pacifica system (WDID 2SSO10100); surface-water-reaching spills only. Reported spills do not explain the chronic dry-weather signal; they are plotted so that can be checked.
What this page does not claim
Correlation is evidence for hypotheses, not proof of mechanism. Each view states what it predicts; the project findings carry falsifiable tests, including a dated prediction for summer 2027 recorded before this El Niño winter.
Analysis pipeline, findings v1–v8, and source registry: github.com/augers-co/pacifica-beach-water. Data: CEDEN/BeachWatch, lindamarwaterquality.org, CIWQS, ERA5, USGS. Creek measurements are the primary signal in this project; beach stations are shown for context.
